title: Pain the medicine
hook: pain became the medicine and pleasure the disease (Asa di Var, ang 469)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sach: a true heart, and truth as medicine for everyone. Today's salok turns the medicine upside down.

Ask people when they changed the most, and very few will name the year everything went well. They'll name the breakup, the layoff, the hospital waiting room, the year a parent died. Nobody would choose those seasons, or wish them on anyone. And yet, looking back, many people say: that's when I woke up. That's when I found out who my friends were, or what I believed. Guru Nanak put that strange experience into one line of the Asa di Var, and it still startles people.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU CHANGE THE MOST?` → `NOBODY CHOOSES THOSE SEASONS.` → `ONE STARTLING LINE.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 469. Its opening line, in paraphrase: pain has become the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no longing for you. Dukh daaroo, sukh rog. Dukh is pain, sorrow, suffering. Daaroo is medicine. Sukh is comfort, pleasure, ease. Rog is disease. This line is easy to misread, so slow down. Guru Nanak isn't saying pain is good, or that people deserve to suffer, or that anyone should go looking for it. Sikh teaching doesn't praise hurting yourself; the Gurus turned away from harsh self-punishment as a path. And in Sikh life, relieving other people's pain is a duty: the langar feeds the hungry, and Sikhs have long run free kitchens and clinics in disasters. The line is about what comfort can do to the heart. When everything is easy, it's easy to forget the One. Ease can make us sleepy. Pain, the salok says, often does the opposite. It breaks the illusion that we're in control, and turns the heart toward the One. Then the salok goes on, still in paraphrase: you are the Doer; I am nothing; if I try to do it myself, nothing happens. And a line that connects back to day five hundred forty-two: I am a sacrifice to you, dwelling in your kudrat, your creation; your limits can't be known. So the medicine isn't the pain itself. It's what pain can open: the end of pretending we run the world, and a turn toward the One who does.
screen: `DUKH DAAROO, SUKH ROG.` · `NOT: PAIN IS GOOD.` · `EASE CAN MAKE US FORGET.` · `YOU ARE THE DOER.` · then, large: `PAIN THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Think of a hard season that is now behind you, not the hardest, and not one that still feels raw; if nothing comes, just rest in the breath. If one does, don't relive it; ask one quiet question, what did that season turn me toward, and let the answer be small. If you pray, say Waheguru, for what you learned and for who helped.
Dukh, pain or sorrow: in Guru Nanak's salok, dukh daaroo, sukh rog, pain can turn the heart toward the One, while ease can make it forget.
Your line: you are the Doer. The medicine is what pain can open. Five hundred fifty days, and counting.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and many recall dukh daaroo, sukh rog in hard times as a reminder that suffering can turn the heart toward the One.

chat.says: Does Guru Nanak's line mean pain is good, and we should go looking for it?
options: No, pain isn't praised; it can turn the heart toward the One, while ease can make it forget.
Yes, it means comfort is a sin, so people who are doing well are far from the One.
No, it means pain is only bad luck, with nothing in it that could turn a heart.
chat.meaning: Dukh daaroo, sukh rog: pain can break the illusion of control and turn the heart toward the One. Sikh teaching never praises hurting yourself.
